extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent practitioners, and members of the public assessing U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility under the 2014 Interim Guidance
extracted.subtask_description: An index of worked examples tied to the USPTO 2014 Interim Guidance on subject-matter eligibility (Step 1 / Step 2A / Step 2B) to help determine whether claimed subject matter is a statutory category, whether it recites a judicial exception, how the MDC analysis characterizes the claim, and which 'significantly more' considerations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory Category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which statutory category the claim recites (e.g., Process, Machine, Manufacture, Composition, System, or CRM). The examples list the applicable category for each claim to establish whether the claim initially falls within a statutory category under 35 U.S.C. §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columns indicate for each example the relevant statutory categories (Process, Machine, Manufacture, Composition, System, CRM). Examples in the appendix show claims labeled as Process, System, Composition, Manufacture, Machine or Manufacture, etc. Use this determination as the first step of the eligibility framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Identify Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim recites a judicial exception (for example, an Abstract Idea or a Product of Nature) or contains no judicial exception ('None' or 'n/a').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Step 2A 'Exception' column classifies each example as Abstract Idea, Product of Nature, None, n/a, Streamlined (Particular Machine), Streamlined (Product of Nature), or similar labels. This determination (that a claim recites a judicial exception vs. not) directs whether to proceed to the MDC analysis and Step 2B. Use the example mappings to quickly locate situations pertinent to a claimed exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: MDC Analysis (characteristics evaluated)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a judicial exception is identified, perform the MDC (Meaningful Distinction/Characteristics) analysis to characterize the exception by attributes such as function/activity, chemical/physical property, structure or form, phenotype, or by whether it is tied to a particular machine/streamlined form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Step 2A 'MDC Analysis' column records the characteristics discussed for each example, e.g., function/activity; chem/phys property; structure or form; phenotype; particular machine; streamlined (Particular Machine) or Streamlined (Product of Nature). Use these characterizations to evaluate whether the claim elements are merely descriptive of a judicial exception or instead present a claim-specific manifestation (e.g., a particular machine, a structured composition, or a transformed composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: 'Significantly More' Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole includes additional elements or a combination of elements that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception, based on a set of considerations (e.g., improving another technology, improving the functioning of a computer, meaningful limitations, transformation, or whether limitations are merely well-understood, routine, and conventional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Step 2B column lists considerations and example outcomes used to determine 'significantly more'. Items and phrasings appearing in the examples include: improving another technology; improving computer; transformation; other meaningful limitations; limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (parenthetical: generic computer performing generic computer functions); mere instructions to 'apply' it; insignificant extra-solution activity; field of use; limitation that is not well-understood, routine, and conventional; no additional elements (i.e., none); streamlined (Product of Nature); streamlined (Particular Machine). Examples show these considerations applied to specific claims (e.g., 'Improving computer, improving another technology, other meaningful limitations, limitation that is well-understood, routine, and conventional (generic computer performing generic computer functions)' or 'Mere instructions to apply it', etc.). Use these considerations to decide whether the additional elements transform the exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
